title: A missing underscore sent innocent man to prison for 18 months
gist: A single-character error in a Wisconsin sheriff's subpoena to Kik (requesting "fus_ro_dah" instead of the real suspect's "fus__ro_dah") caused Canadian police to arrest, convict, and imprison the wrong man, Brandon Klayme, for 18 months before an appeal uncovered the mistake.

themes.theme: Subpoena error and platform data handoff

insights.claim: A one-character discrepancy in a law-enforcement subpoena to Kik messaging service (requesting username "fus_ro_dah" instead of the actual suspect's "fus__ro_dah", which has a double underscore) caused the platform to hand over an innocent Canadian man's email address instead of the real perpetrator's.
insights.speaker: Nate Anderson
insights.so_what: Illustrates how messaging/identity platforms' subpoena-response pipelines have no secondary verification step, so a single typo in a legal request can misdirect an entire criminal investigation with no platform-side check.
insights.quote: their subpoena accidentally requested information about the Kik user “fus_ro_dah” (one underscore after “fus”). Kik provided Klayme’s email address in response.

insights.claim: Once Kik supplied the mismatched email address, the error propagated automatically across multiple downstream data providers: Google account IP logs, Canadian ISP Bell Aliant's subscriber records, and finally a physical residential address, without any party re-checking the original username.
insights.speaker: Nate Anderson
insights.so_what: Shows how chained third-party data requests (platform to platform to ISP to police) compound an initial identity error rather than catching it, a systemic risk in any investigation reliant on cross-company subpoena chains.
insights.locator: Google records showed that this email address was used to access Google services

insights.claim: Despite a forensic search of Brandon Klayme's phones and laptops turning up no evidence linking him to the victim, no intimate images, and no proof he even used Kik during the relevant period, he was still arrested and charged with three offenses including child luring and possession of child pornography.
insights.speaker: Nate Anderson
insights.so_what: A cautionary case study in how digital-identity evidence (subpoena-derived usernames/IPs) can override the absence of corroborating device evidence in prosecutorial decision-making.
insights.locator: Searching these devices produced no evidence relevant to the case

insights.claim: The underscore discrepancy between the real suspect's and Klayme's usernames was never caught by police, prosecutors, defense counsel, or the trial judge during Klayme's 2023 trial, and the court could not later explain how it went unnoticed for years.
insights.speaker: Nate Anderson
insights.so_what: Highlights a verification gap across the entire justice pipeline for digital-identity evidence — no single actor in the chain independently re-validated the platform-provided identifiers before conviction.
insights.quote: Although the information about the usernames was available at the time of the trial, there is no evidence confirming or explaining how it went unnoticed.
insights.locator: How could such a crucial mistake have been missed

themes.theme: Appeal, exoneration, and the real suspect

insights.claim: Brandon Klayme was convicted in 2023, sentenced in 2024 to 18 months in prison, served the full term, and only had his conviction overturned by the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal after his own appeal team discovered the username mismatch late in the appeals process.
insights.speaker: Nate Anderson
insights.so_what: Concrete timeline (2018 investigation to 2020 arrest to 2023 conviction to 2024 sentencing to 2026 acquittal) shows the multi-year cost of an unverified digital-identity error before self-correction.
insights.quote: Mr. Klayme is factually innocent of the offences. He should never have been charged, let alone convicted.

insights.claim: Had investigators requested the correct double-underscore username, evidence would have pointed to a different individual whose first name is Jay and whose IP address appears to be in California — meaning the actual suspect from a Wisconsin child-luring case was never identified or apprehended.
insights.speaker: Nate Anderson
insights.so_what: The true perpetrator in the underlying 2018 child-luring case remains unidentified and at large, an unresolved public-safety loose end the story leaves open.
insights.quote: would have identified an individual whose first name is Jay whose IP address appears to be in California.
insights.locator: After this was pointed out, prosecutors took another look
